steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Tension: pulling force that stretches - ropes, cables, bridge wires. Compression: pushing force that squashes - columns, arches, foam packaging.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Bending: combines tension (outer surface stretches) and compression (inner surface squashes) - I-beams concentrate material at flanges where forces are greatest.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Shear: forces in opposite directions parallel to a surface - scissors, bolted joints. Torsion: twisting force - drive shafts, screwdrivers.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Stress = Force / Area (N/m2). Strain = Change in length / Original length. Young's Modulus = Stress / Strain (measures stiffness).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: A shelf supports books. Explain where tension and compression occur in the shelf when loaded. | Explain why an I-beam is more efficient than a solid rectangular beam of the same weight. | A crane cable has UTS of 800 MPa and working stress of 200 MPa. Calculate the factor of safety and explain whether this is appropriate.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Top surface is in compression (squashed as the shelf bends downward), bottom surface is in tension (stretched as it curves). The centre (neutral axis) has zero stress. Shelf supports are often L-shape | In bending, stress is highest at top and bottom surfaces, zero at the neutral axis. An I-beam concentrates material in the flanges (top/bottom) where stress is highest, and minimises material in the w | FoS = 800 / 200 = 4. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always annotate diagrams showing tension, compression and neutral axis State the formula before calculating: FoS = UTS / Working stress Relate forces back to product design decisions
